questions.question: Which broad area takes the largest share of UK public spending?

options.B: Social protection, including pensions and benefits

questions.why: HM Treasury PESA consistently shows social protection as the largest function of spending.

questions.question: Roughly how large is total UK public spending compared with the size of the whole economy (GDP)?
questions.why: OBR and HM Treasury figures put total managed expenditure at roughly 40-45% of GDP in recent decades.

questions.question: After social protection, which area usually receives the most UK public spending?
questions.why: PESA shows health as the second-largest spending function, well ahead of defence or policing.

questions.question: Spending on a service rose 20% in cash over ten years while prices rose 25%. What happened after inflation?
questions.why: When prices rise faster than cash spending, real (inflation-adjusted) spending falls.

questions.question: Which single tax raises the most money for the UK government?
questions.why: HMRC and OBR figures show income tax is the largest single source of receipts.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three biggest UK revenue raisers?
questions.why: Income tax, National Insurance and VAT are the three largest; fuel duty raises far less.

questions.question: When the government spends more than it receives in taxes and other receipts, how is the gap covered?

options.C: By counting it as tax revenue

questions.why: The gap is public sector net borrowing, which is not a tax or a receipt.

questions.question: Roughly what share of all income tax is paid by the top 1% of income taxpayers?
questions.why: HMRC income tax statistics show the top 1% pay well over a quarter of income tax.

questions.question: As a share of their disposable income, who pays more in indirect taxes such as VAT?

options.C: Both pay exactly the same share

questions.why: ONS 'Effects of taxes and benefits' shows indirect taxes take a larger share of disposable income for poorer households.

questions.question: Which group of households pays the most tax in pounds, on average?

options.D: All fifths pay the same amount

questions.why: ONS data show the richest fifth pay the most total tax in cash terms.

questions.question: A chart says households pay, on average, about a third of gross income in all taxes. What does this mean?

options.B: An average across households, combining direct and indirect taxes
options.C: A third of government revenue comes from income tax
options.D: Every household pays exactly a third

questions.why: A household average of combined taxes is not a personal tax rate or a share of total revenue.

questions.question: Income tax raises roughly a quarter of all government receipts. What does that tell you about your own income tax?

options.A: You pay 25% of your income in income tax
options.B: You pay a quarter of your taxes as income tax
options.C: A quarter of people pay income tax
options.D: Nothing directly; a share of revenue is not a personal tax rate

questions.why: A tax's share of total revenue is a different measure from the rate any individual pays.

questions.question: Which of these is an indirect tax?
questions.why: VAT is paid through spending, so ONS classes it as indirect; the others are direct taxes.

questions.question: In ONS household statistics, what is 'disposable income'?

options.A: Income left after direct taxes, including cash benefits
options.B: Income before any taxes or benefits
options.D: Income after rent or mortgage payments

questions.why: ONS defines disposable income as gross income (including cash benefits) minus direct taxes.

questions.question: A page shows 'an illustrative household earning £30,000' and its tax bill. What is this?

options.C: A worked example based on stated assumptions, not a measured statistic
options.D: An official HMRC record for a real family

questions.why: An illustration shows how rules apply under assumptions; it is not measured evidence about real households.

questions.question: Employment rose in the years after a new policy began. From that fact alone, what can you conclude?

options.C: Employment would have fallen without it
options.D: Employment rose, but this alone does not show why

questions.why: A change over time does not prove its cause; other factors could explain it.

questions.question: A survey chart shows a gap for 2020 because data were not collected. How should you read the gap?

options.A: The value was zero that year
options.B: The value was halfway between 2019 and 2021
options.C: There is no comparable figure for that year
options.D: The value was the same as 2019

questions.why: A missing year means no measurement; it should not be treated as zero or filled in.

questions.question: A line jumps sharply in the year a statistic's definition changed. What is the safest reading?

options.A: Part or all of the jump may reflect the change in definition
options.B: The jump shows a real change in people's lives
options.C: The older figures were simply wrong
options.D: The new definition always makes numbers bigger

questions.why: A break in a series means figures either side are not directly comparable.

questions.question: What does the UK employment rate measure?

options.A: The share of job-seekers who cannot find work
options.B: The share of people aged 16 to 64 who are in paid work
options.D: The share of adults claiming benefits

questions.why: ONS defines the headline employment rate as the proportion of people aged 16 to 64 in employment.

questions.question: Average pay rose 5% in cash over a year while prices rose 7%. What happened to real pay?
questions.why: Real pay change is roughly cash growth minus inflation, so 5% - 7% is about -2%.

questions.question: To compare average pay in 1998 with pay today fairly, which figures should you use?

options.A: Cash pay, as written on payslips at the time
options.B: Pay in whichever year was highest
options.C: Pay before tax only, with no other change

questions.why: Prices change over time, so only inflation-adjusted pay shows what earnings could buy across periods.

questions.question: In England, what is the most common way households occupy their homes?

options.A: Owner occupation (owned outright or with a mortgage)

questions.why: The English Housing Survey shows around two thirds of households are owner occupiers.

questions.question: Which country do UK residents visit most often on trips abroad?
questions.why: ONS Travel trends consistently show Spain as the top destination for UK residents' visits abroad.

questions.question: In England, the law limits infant classes (ages 5 to 7) with one teacher to how many pupils?
questions.why: The infant class size limit in England is 30 pupils per school teacher.
